questions.q: What is a Big Object purpose-built for?
options: Running real-time Apex triggers at very high frequency
Replacing Account and Opportunity as the org's primary working objects
Encrypting sensitive fields at rest
Storing and managing massive numbers of records cheaply, while keeping that data retrievable through a query when genuinely needed
questions.explain: Big Objects exist to hold volumes of data too large to keep affordably in standard or custom objects, while still allowing that data to be retrieved later through a query — which is exactly what makes them a natural archiving target.

questions.q: Which of these is a real, documented constraint on Big Objects?
options: Big Objects support a narrower set of field types (commonly DateTime, Lookup, Number, Text, Long Text Area) and don't support the upsert operation
Big Objects support unlimited custom field types, identical to standard objects
Big Objects cannot be queried at all once created
Big Objects automatically convert into standard objects after one year
questions.explain: Big Objects support a narrower set of field types than standard/custom objects, don't support upsert, and have much more limited trigger/flow support — all real constraints an architect has to design around.

questions.q: Why does this lesson caution against assuming a specific Big Object query mechanism described in older documentation is still the current supported approach?
options: Because Big Objects were never actually released as a real feature
Because Salesforce's own documentation announced Async SOQL, a batch-style way to query Big Objects, for retirement — so a mechanism named in older material isn't guaranteed to still be current
Because Big Objects can only be queried through the user interface, never programmatically
Because query tooling for Big Objects has never changed since the feature launched
questions.explain: Async SOQL, a previously documented way to query Big Objects at scale, was announced for retirement by Salesforce — a clear example of why an architect should confirm the currently supported method rather than assume older documentation still applies.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does a Big Object earn its place as an archive target over a simpler external system (data warehouse, backup platform)?
options: Only when the data will never be queried again
Whenever an org has more than 100 custom objects already
When the data volume is too large for a practical external round-trip every time it might be needed, but it still needs to stay queryable from inside Salesforce itself
Only for data created in the last 30 days
questions.explain: A Big Object is the right choice specifically when volume makes repeated external round-trips impractical but in-Salesforce queryability still matters — for lower-volume or rarely-needed historical data, an external system may be simpler and avoid Big Object constraints entirely.

questions.q: Why is Big Objects' restricted trigger and Flow automation support described as "generally appropriate" rather than purely a downside?
options: Because automation is never useful on any Salesforce object
Because Flow doesn't exist as a Salesforce feature
Because triggers are being deprecated across the entire platform
Because Big Objects are meant to hold settled, historical data rather than data that needs ongoing business-process automation reacting to it
questions.explain: Since Big Objects are meant for settled historical/archived data rather than live, actively-changing business data, the reduced need for ongoing trigger/Flow automation against it fits the object type's actual purpose.
